title: The Commercial and Political Atlas
authority: Playfair, a Scottish engineer and political economist, invented the line chart, bar chart (1786) and pie chart (1801), the founding act of statistical graphics.
caveats: Historical origin source, not empirical evidence. Later editions (1787, 1801) add material; the pie chart appears in the 1801 Statistical Breviary.

title: Graphical perception: Theory, experimentation, and application to the development of graphical methods
container: Journal of the American Statistical Association
authority: Bell Labs statisticians whose experiments created the empirical ranking of elementary perceptual tasks that underlies most chart-choice guidance.
caveats: Small lab samples; position-length-angle ranking replicated by Heer and Bostock 2010, but angle vs area ordering and pie-chart results are nuanced (Spence, Lewandowsky). Tasks were accuracy of ratio judgment only.

title: Crowdsourcing graphical perception: Using Mechanical Turk to assess visualization design
container: Proceedings of the SIGCHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI 2010)
authority: Stanford/Berkeley HCI researchers (Bostock later created D3); CHI Honorable Mention paper that validated crowdsourced perception studies and replicated Cleveland and McGill.
caveats: Online workers on uncontrolled displays; new experiments (rectangle area, chart size, gridlines) cover simple charts only; numeric details beyond the abstract not confirmed here.

title: The Visual Display of Quantitative Information
authority: Statistician and Yale professor; the most influential modern statement of graphical integrity, data-ink and small multiples.
caveats: Data-ink maximization is a heuristic, not an experimental finding; Bateman 2010 and Borkin 2013 show embellishment can aid memory. Specific numeric thresholds quoted in secondary sources were not confirmed against the book.

title: Semiologie graphique: Les diagrammes, les reseaux, les cartes
edition: English: Semiology of Graphics, trans. W. J. Berg, University of Wisconsin Press, 1983
authority: French cartographer who defined the visual variables and levels of organization; foundation of all later encoding taxonomies.
caveats: Theory built from cartographic experience with little experimental testing; some rankings later revised by Cleveland and McGill and Mackinlay.

title: Exploratory Data Analysis
authority: Princeton and Bell Labs statistician who founded exploratory analysis and introduced the box plot and stem-and-leaf display.
caveats: Exploratory methods are for analysts; idiosyncratic terminology; inference left to confirmatory work.

title: Automating the design of graphical presentations of relational information
authority: Stanford PhD work (APT) that formalized expressiveness and effectiveness criteria and ranked encodings per data type; basis of Tableau's Show Me.
caveats: Rankings for ordinal and nominal data are partly extrapolated from Cleveland and McGill, not tested directly.

title: The eyes have it: A task by data type taxonomy for information visualizations
container: Proceedings of the IEEE Symposium on Visual Languages
authority: University of Maryland HCI pioneer; the paper that gave the field the overview first, zoom and filter, details on demand mantra.
caveats: A design taxonomy, not an experiment; mantra is a heuristic and has been extended (e.g., Craft and Cairns critique of its evidence). DOI not confirmed this session, so left blank.

title: Bars and lines: A study of graphic communication
authority: Cognitive psychologists at Stanford; experiments showing viewers describe bars as discrete categories and lines as trends.
caveats: Small studies on undergraduates; a strong tendency, not a rule, and later work (Zacks and Tversky; Shah) refines it. DOI not confirmed this session, so left blank.

title: Useful junk? The effects of visual embellishment on comprehension and memorability of charts
container: Proceedings of the SIGCHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI 2010)
authority: University of Saskatchewan HCI group; the first controlled test of Tufte's chartjunk claims.
caveats: Small lab sample (a secondary critique reports 20 students and 14 charts; not confirmed against the paper). Recall advantage appears at a delay of roughly two to three weeks per summaries (exact interval not confirmed). Accuracy was not worse with embellishment. Not replicated at scale; Holmes-style illustrations only.

title: What makes a visualization memorable?
container: IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics
authority: Harvard and MIT vision and visualization researchers; large-scale memorability study with eye tracking.
caveats: Memorability (recognition after a very brief exposure) is not comprehension; the authors say a memorable visualization is not necessarily a good one. Single study family; follow-up work (Borkin et al. 2016) examines recall of messages.

title: Information Dashboard Design: The Effective Visual Communication of Data
authority: Practitioner and educator whose critique of gauges and decoration defined modern dashboard design; invented the bullet graph.
caveats: Opinionated and practice-derived, not experimental; his hostility to gauges is for dense business dashboards and does not directly settle instrument-like displays for training.

title: Visualization Analysis and Design
authority: University of British Columbia professor; standard textbook with the what-why-how framework and the nested model of design validation.
caveats: Textbook synthesis; effectiveness rankings inherited from Cleveland and McGill, Mackinlay and Heer and Bostock.

title: The Grammar of Graphics
authority: Statistician (SPSS, SYSTAT) whose formal grammar underlies ggplot2, Vega-Lite and Tableau.
caveats: A specification system, not perceptual guidance; says what charts can be built, not which are good.

title: The science of visual data communication: What works
container: Psychological Science in the Public Interest
authority: Five leading vision and visualization scientists; the current evidence review for the field.
caveats: Review of mixed-quality studies; authors flag many open questions and context dependence.

title: Hypothetical outcome plots outperform error bars and violin plots for inferences about reliability of variable ordering
authority: Hullman is the leading researcher on uncertainty visualization; this paper tested animated draws against static uncertainty displays.
caveats: Task is narrow (judging ordering reliability); animation cost and accessibility concerns; not about learners. DOI not confirmed this session, so left blank.
